request:
Spike: verify node:sqlite WAL and npm min-release-age behaviour

With real Node 24.x, confirm:

- `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` works with `node:sqlite`, including a concurrent reader during a write transaction
- `min-release-age=7` blocks installing a version younger than 7 days, and how exclusions work

Record the findings in the relevant ADR or DEPENDENCIES.md.

Project scaffolding: package.json, tsconfig, Biome, folder layout

Set up the TypeScript project per ADR 0001 and ADR 0004.

- `package.json`: `type: module`, `engines.node >=24.15`, no `pre*`/`post*` scripts (lifecycle scripts are disabled by `.npmrc`)
- `tsconfig.json`: `strict`, `erasableSyntaxOnly`, `verbatimModuleSyntax`, `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`, `module: nodenext`
- Dev dependencies admitted per the DEPENDENCIES.md checklist: `typescript`, `@types/node`, `@biomejs/biome` (exact versions, at least 7 days old)
- Folder layout from docs/architecture.md §14
- Scripts: `typecheck`, `lint`, `test` (`node --test`)

**Done when:** `npm ci && npm run typecheck && npm run lint && npm test` pass on a clean clone; `npm ls --all` shows only admitted packages.

Local gate: npm run check and a pre-push Claude Code hook

One local gate, enforced before anything leaves the machine.

- Add `"check": "npm run typecheck && npm run lint && npm test"` to `package.json`, if #1 has not already added it.
- Add a project hook in `.claude/settings.json`: a `PreToolUse` hook on `Bash` that runs `npm run check` before `git push` and `gh pr create`, and blocks the command when the check fails.
- No git hooks. They would need an install script, and `package.json` allows no `pre*`/`post*` scripts.
- The hook command must work in PowerShell, Git Bash, macOS and Linux shells. Prefer a small Node script (`scripts/precheck.ts`) over shell syntax.

**Done when:** a push with a failing test is blocked in a Claude Code session on Windows and Linux, and `CLAUDE.md` documents the hook.

Review skill for Foedrum's own pull requests

A Claude Code skill in `.claude/skills/brew-review/` (named `brew-review`, because `review` collides with a built-in command) that every pull request to Foedrum goes through while it is a draft. It turns the review routine into a repeatable recipe and leaves evidence on the pull request. Design: [ADR 0017](https://github.com/EdwinBekaert/foedrum/blob/main/docs/adr/0017-test-first-recipes-and-tasting-lenses.md).

Stages, in order. Each reviewer runs in a **fresh subagent** that receives only the diff, `CLAUDE.md` and the ADRs the diff touches, never the context of the session that wrote the code:

1. **Red proof** — check out each test commit before its implementation commit, run the tests, and confirm they fail *in the new tests*. A compile or import error does not count as red. Exempt: spikes, scaffolding, docs, CI configuration.
2. **Simplify** — remove duplication and unneeded code; tests stay green.
3. **Lens reviews**, one subagent per lens, read from `defaults/lenses/*.md`:
   - correctness and invariants (I1–I6, "every wait has a deadline")
   - security (untrusted issue text, the Windows shell spawn, secrets)
   - cross-platform (paths, spawning, line endings, file locks)
   - design conformance (ADRs, glossary terms, dependency policy)
4. **Mutation check (Brett)** — in a scratch worktree, introduce 3–5 plausible bugs in the changed code, one at a time, run the tests and report every mutant that survives.
5. **Coverage delta** — `node --test --experimental-test-coverage` on the changed files.
6. **Summary comment** on the pull request: each finding with its disposition (fixed in <commit> / dismissed because …), surviving mutants, coverage delta.

The lens files are written so Foedrum's default Taster can use the same files later. Foedrum reviews its own pull requests with the prompts it ships.

**Done when:**
- `/brew-review` on a draft pull request produces the summary comment.
- Running it on a pull request with a planted defect (missing deadline, string-built path) reports that defect.
- A pull request whose tests were written after the code fails the red proof.


**Reviewers are read-only agents that mirror the default brewers:** `.claude/agents/taster.md` (Read, Grep, Glob; opus, medium), one run per lens, and `.claude/agents/brett.md` (Read, Grep, Glob; sonnet, medium), which only proposes mutants. The main session writes the diff to `.foedrum/tmp/<issue>/`, then applies and runs the mutants and the tests itself. That way text injected into a pull request can't make a reviewer push or post.

JSONC reader and JSON frontmatter parser

Small in-house parsers per ADR 0007.

- JSONC: strip `//` and `/* */` comments and trailing commas, string-aware (comment-like text inside strings untouched), then `JSON.parse`; errors report line and column
- Frontmatter: a JSON object between `---` lines at the top of a Markdown file; tolerant of CRLF and a BOM

**Done when:** table-driven tests cover strings containing comment markers, escapes, nesting, CRLF, BOM and malformed input.

CI: test matrix on Windows, macOS and Linux

GitHub Actions workflow per ADR 0004 and ADR 0010.

- Matrix: `ubuntu-latest`, `macos-latest`, `windows-latest` × Node 24 and the current LTS
- All actions pinned to full commit SHAs; `permissions: contents: read`
- Steps: npm version check (≥ 11.16), `npm ci`, `npm audit signatures`, `npm audit --omit=dev`, typecheck, lint, test

**Done when:** every pull request runs the full matrix and fails on any red step.

### Actions minutes while the repository is private

Private repositories have a limited monthly Actions budget, and macOS minutes count 10×, Windows 2×. Until the repository is public (M3):

- **Pull requests:** `ubuntu-latest` + `windows-latest` only
- **Push to `main` and nightly:** the full matrix including `macos-latest`
- Cancel superseded runs (`concurrency` with `cancel-in-progress`) and cache the npm cache directory
- Keep the PR test suite fast; the 1,000-run chaos suite (#15) runs nightly on Linux only
- When the repository becomes public, switch pull requests to the full matrix

Locally, contributors cover Windows natively and Linux through WSL2; macOS is covered by CI only.


### Quality gates

- CI runs the same `npm run check` as contributors do locally (#24), plus the audit steps above.
- **Coverage thresholds** with Node's built-in coverage, no extra dependency: `node --test --experimental-test-coverage --test-coverage-lines=90 --test-coverage-branches=85 --test-coverage-functions=90`. The run fails below the thresholds. Start at the current level if it is lower, and only ever raise them.
- Coverage summary written to the job summary (`$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`).
- The required status check is a single aggregate job (`ci-ok`) that depends on the whole matrix, so branch rules do not need to list every matrix entry.

**Branch rules for `main`.** Rulesets on private personal repositories need GitHub Pro, so switch these on when the repository becomes public (M3), or earlier with Pro:
- require a pull request, and `ci-ok` passing
- merge commits only (no squash, no rebase), so red → green history stays on `main`; no linear-history rule
- block force-pushes and deletion

Dependency guard: lockfile checker and Dependabot cooldown

A zero-dependency `scripts/check-deps.ts` (run with Node type stripping) that fails when:

- any `resolved` URL is not under `https://registry.npmjs.org/`
- any entry lacks `integrity`
- any package has `hasInstallScript: true`
- the package budget is exceeded (runtime ≤ 2, total ≤ 10)
- a package is not listed in DEPENDENCIES.md

Plus `.github/dependabot.yml` for npm and github-actions with a 7-day cooldown, grouped weekly.

**Done when:** the checker runs in CI and has tests for each failure rule.

Schemas: events, step outcomes, out docs, recipes, brewers, config

Zod schemas as the single source for TypeScript types, runtime validation and JSON Schema (ADR 0004, ADR 0005).

- Events (architecture §4.1), `StepOutcome` (§4.2), the out-doc frontmatter contract (brewers-and-recipes §2)
- Multi-repository model: orders, sub-orders, dependencies (`code` / `release`), bottles
- Generate JSON Schema files for editor autocompletion

Recipe, brewer frontmatter, `foedrum.jsonc` and `models.jsonc` moved to #52.

**Done when:** every schema has valid and invalid fixture tests, and JSON Schema generation is reproducible.

Test-design lens: catch tests that test the tool, cannot fail, or are slow

Add a fifth default lens, **test-design**, so reviews catch tests that test the wrong thing, cannot fail, or are slow, before they pile up. Seen in this wave: unit tests that build real git repositories (#51, now ADR 0021), rejection tests that passed against a reject-everything `z.never()` stub (#47), a success-path test that passed against a stub with no entry point (#46).

The deterministic part (no process in `test/unit/`, per-file time budget) is in #58; this lens covers what needs judgement.

## Lens: `defaults/lenses/test-design.md`

Look for:
- **Testing the tool instead of our code:** git, npm, a shell or `claude` started in a unit test; decisions that should sit in a pure core tested with data (ADR 0021).
- **Tests that cannot fail:** passing against a no-op or reject-everything stub; assertions inside a callback that never runs; missing `await`; always-true conditions; asserting only that a mock was called.
- **Red for the wrong reason:** a missing file, import or compile error instead of missing behaviour; stubs that return a value instead of throwing `not implemented` (#25, #36).
- **Slow or heavy tests:** real directory trees or repositories where data would do, sleeps, wide timeouts, retries in tests.
- **Fixtures:** tool output written by hand instead of captured; no integration test proving a fixture still matches the real tool.
- **Behaviour coverage:** a new behaviour no test would catch breaking; untested error paths and edge cases. Move the "Tests" section of `defaults/lenses/correctness.md` here, and point correctness to this lens, so the two do not overlap.

## Also
- **ADR 0022:** five default lenses (amends the list in ADR 0017). Update `docs/brewers-and-recipes.md` and `docs/architecture.md` where lenses are listed.
- **brew-review:** run the new lens with the others.
- **Planted-defect sample:** add two test-design defects to `test/fixtures/brew-review/planted-demo` (a unit test that runs git; a rejection test that passes against a reject-everything stub) and their expected findings.
- **One source for the rules:** the Gauger's instructions (#25) will reference this lens's checklist instead of repeating it; leave a note on #25.

## Verification
Prompt changes are exempt from red proof but not from verification (CLAUDE.md): run `/brew-review` against the planted-defect sample and show that the test-design lens reports both planted defects, and that correctness no longer reports test findings.

**Done when:** the lens ships in `defaults/lenses/`, brew-review runs it, and the planted-demo run finds both planted defects.

Clean up merged worktrees and branches automatically

Every issue session leaves its worktree and local branch behind after the pull request merges, and removing them by hand fails on Windows (ReadOnly attributes, files held open, stale entries under `.git/worktrees/`). Nobody owns the step: Claude Code keeps a worktree that has commits, and the session ends before the merge. Cleanup should need no human.

The engine needs the same thing for batch worktrees, so the deletion logic belongs in the platform layer (#12) and this issue is its first user.

## Scope

**`scripts/worktrees-clean.ts`, run as `npm run worktrees:clean`:**
- `git fetch --prune origin` first.
- Candidates: worktrees under `.claude/worktrees/` only (never the main checkout, never anything outside it), and local branches without a worktree.
- Removable when the branch tip is an ancestor of `origin/main`. Merges are merge commits (no squash), so this is exact and needs no GitHub API call.
- Never remove a worktree that:
  - has uncommitted or untracked changes (`git status --porcelain`), or
  - is locked by a live session: the lock reason is `claude session <name> (pid <n>)`, so skip it while that pid is alive, and unlock it when the pid is gone.
- Remove in this order: clear ReadOnly (Windows), unlock, `git worktree remove`, `git worktree prune`, `git branch -d` (never `-D`), then delete the remote branch if it still exists and is merged.
- Retry deletes that fail with EBUSY, EPERM or ENOTEMPTY, with a short backoff (a few attempts), then report the path and carry on. Never prompt; never fail the session.
- Print one line per removed or skipped item, with the reason.

**Automatic:** a `SessionStart` hook in `.claude/settings.json` that runs it only when `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` is the main checkout (not inside a worktree), in the background or with a short timeout, so starting `claude` is not slowed down.

**Platform layer (#12):** the robust delete (clear ReadOnly, retry on busy files) lives in `src/platform/` with tests, and the script imports it. #12's "clear the read-only attribute before deleting" item is done here.

## Test-first

Tests build real temporary repositories under `.foedrum/tmp/` (with a bare repo as `origin`) and cover:
- a merged branch with a worktree is removed, worktree, local branch and remote branch;
- an unmerged branch, a dirty worktree and a worktree locked by a live pid are kept;
- a lock whose pid is dead is unlocked and removed;
- a stale `.git/worktrees/<name>` entry whose folder is gone is pruned;
- on Windows: a worktree with ReadOnly files is removed; a busy file is retried, then reported without failing.

## Done when

After a pull request merges, the next `claude` started in the main checkout leaves no worktree, local branch or remote branch of it, with no command typed by hand, on Windows, macOS and Linux.

Domain model and fold

A pure fold from events to state (architecture §4).

- Orders, sub-orders (one repository each), dependencies, batches, steps, attempts, bottles
- Deterministic: the same events always produce the same state

**Done when:** replay tests and invariant I3 (replay yields identical state) hold.

EventStore on node:sqlite

Local store and index per ADR 0002 and ADR 0011, behind an `EventStore` interface.

- Tables: events (append-only), leases (mutable), effects (idempotency ledger with a `UNIQUE` key)
- WAL mode, busy timeout, a `withTransaction` helper (`BEGIN IMMEDIATE` / `COMMIT` / `ROLLBACK`)
- Queries: events after id N, batches past their deadline, current leases

**Done when:** tests prove an atomic append + lease + effect in one transaction, a rejected duplicate effect, and reads during a write.

Effect key, EffectKey and Lease as zod schemas

Follow-up from the review of #63 (EventStore on node:sqlite). The design-conformance finding was dismissed there in favour of this issue.

## Why

#63 makes the `effect.applied` events the idempotency ledger. Each event's `key` is the canonical JSON array `[batchId, stepId, attempt, effect]`. That key is now part of the persisted log, but:

- it is validated by hand in `src/engine/effect-key.ts`;
- `effect.applied.key` in `src/schemas/events.ts` still accepts any non-empty string, so the generated JSON Schema accepts keys that the store rejects;
- `EffectKey` and `Lease` are plain TypeScript interfaces in `src/engine/event-store.ts`.

CLAUDE.md: "Zod schemas in `src/schemas/` are the single source of types, runtime validation and generated JSON Schema." `src/schemas/` was left alone in #63 because #8 was changing it in parallel.

## What

- Move the effect-key tuple into `src/schemas/`, with the canonical refinement: a strict tuple `[Id, Id, positive int, NonEmpty]`, whose text must equal its own canonical encoding.
- Move `EffectKey` and `Lease` there too, and infer their types from the schemas.
- Tighten `effect.applied.key` to the canonical encoding.
- Regenerate the JSON Schema files with `npm run schemas`.
- Make `src/engine/effect-key.ts` use the schema instead of validating by hand. Its tests (`test/unit/effect-key.test.ts`) must stay green, and so must the store's.

## When

Start after both #63 and #62 are merged: this issue changes `src/engine/effect-key.ts`, which #63 adds. Finish before #7 starts: once #7 writes logs to the state branch, a stricter key schema could reject logs that are already stored.

Unit tests start no processes: move process tests to test/integration (ADR 0021)

Apply [ADR 0021](docs/adr/0021-unit-tests-spawn-no-processes.md) (#57) to the existing unit tests that start processes, and add the integration layer.

**Move or rewrite:**
- `test/unit/precheck.test.ts`: runs the gate hook through bash and npm. Test the gate's decisions (which commands are blocked or need `npm run check`) as a pure function on the hook input; keep one or two integration tests that run the real hook command from `.claude/settings.json`. Overlaps with #41 (gate without npm) and #42 (gate hardening).
- `test/unit/secret-scan.test.ts`: runs processes in 4 places.
- `test/unit/check-deps.test.ts`: the CLI tests run the script as a process; test the CLI's argument handling and exit codes through an exported function, and keep one integration test.

**Add:**
- `test/integration/` and `npm run test:integration`.
- A CI step running it on every matrix leg, and in the nightly run.
- A check that `npm run check` stays under the 20 s budget: report its duration in CI, and fail when a single unit test file takes more than a few seconds.

**Done when:** no file under `test/unit/` starts a process, `npm run check` takes under 20 s on Windows, and the integration tests pass on all three operating systems in CI.

brew-review: scratch-tree cleanup fails on Windows ReadOnly records

Found while finishing the review of #51 on Windows.

The brew-review skill's last stage cleans up its scratch tree with `git worktree remove --force "<scratch>/tree"`, an `rmSync` of the scratch folder and `git worktree prune`. On Windows the record under `.git/worktrees/tree` had the ReadOnly attribute (`attrib` shows `R`), and both git commands failed:

```
error: failed to delete 'C:/code/foedrum/.claude/worktrees/49-worktree-cleanup/.foedrum/tmp/49/scratch/tree': Permission denied
error: failed to delete 'C:/code/foedrum/.git/worktrees/tree': Permission denied
```

The `rmSync` removed the folder, but the record stayed, and `git worktree prune` could not remove it either. `removeTree` from `src/platform/remove.ts` (#49) removed it at once, because it clears the read-only bits first.

Once #51 is merged, the session-start cleanup also prunes such a record: it lies inside `.claude/worktrees/`, at any depth. The skill's own cleanup still reports a failure every time, though, and a review run outside a worktree (from the main checkout) leaves a record outside `.claude/worktrees/`, which the cleanup does not touch.

Proposal: in the skill's stage 6 cleanup, remove the scratch tree and its record through the platform removal, for example a small `node` one-liner that imports `removeTree`, or a `scripts/` helper that the skill calls, instead of `git worktree remove --force`, `rmSync` and a repository-wide `git worktree prune`.

npm run check takes 15–19 s locally against 3–6 s in CI

ADR 0021 keeps `npm run check` under 20 s on a developer machine. Since the EventStore tests (#63) came in, it takes **15–19 s locally on Windows**, while CI reports **3–6 s** on every leg (#68's job summary), with the same test count.

That gap is too large to be the tests alone. Find where the local time goes before adding more tests to the engine.

**What to do**
- Time each part of `npm run check` separately on the Windows machine: `tsc`, `biome check`, `npm test` (with and without `--experimental-test-coverage`), `check-test-layers`, `check-deps --offline`. Also time npm's own start-up (`npm run` of an empty script).
- Use the slowest-files list that #68's budget reporter prints, and compare it with CI's.
- Check machine factors with evidence, not guesses: real-time antivirus scanning of the checkout and of `node_modules`, the `.foedrum/tmp/tests` trees the tests create, and parallelism (`--test-concurrency`, CPU count).
- Fix what is ours (a slow test, a missing cleanup, a serial step that could run in parallel). For machine factors, document the fix in CLAUDE.md, for example an antivirus exclusion for the checkout, with the measured difference.

**Done when:** a written breakdown of the local time is in the PR, and `npm run check` takes under 10 s on this machine, or the PR explains with measurements why it can't.

Depends on #68 (the budget reporter).

State branch: durable events and out docs in the Brewery

Durable record per ADR 0011.

- Per batch: `batches/<id>/events.jsonl` and out docs on branch `foedrum/state`, through a dedicated worktree
- Commit and push at every step boundary
- Rebuild the SQLite index from the branch when it is missing or behind
- A rejected (non-fast-forward) push stops the engine: one active engine per Brewery

**Done when:** tests show that deleting the local database rebuilds it identically, and that a simulated concurrent writer stops the engine.

Reinstall node_modules when package-lock.json changed under the main checkout

After a `git pull` in the main checkout that changes `package-lock.json`, `node_modules` there no longer matches the lock file and `npm run check` fails until someone runs `npm ci` by hand. The main checkout matters more than a worktree: the `SessionStart` and `PreToolUse` hooks run `npm run --prefix "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}"`, so a stale tree there can make the gate fail for every session ("Foedrum gate could not run"). The restart procedure in CLAUDE.md tells the user to `git pull` in the main checkout, so this happens after every dependency change.

Sessions must run unattended, so this needs a tooling fix, not a manual step.

**Proposal**
- A pure function decides whether `node_modules` is stale: compare `package-lock.json` with npm's hidden lock file `node_modules/.package-lock.json` (the `packages` entries' versions and integrity, ignoring the root entry). Missing hidden lock file = stale. Unit-test it with data (ADR 0021): equal, changed version, added package, removed package, missing file.
- The `SessionStart` hook (startup|resume) runs `npm ci` in `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` when the tree is stale, **before** the worktree cleanup and **synchronously**, so no gate runs against a half-installed tree. `npm ci` is already allowed in `.claude/settings.json`; the hook runs it directly, so no permission prompt.
- The gate (`scripts/precheck.ts`) runs the same staleness check first and, when stale, blocks with one clear line ("node_modules is out of date with package-lock.json; run npm ci") instead of failing on an import error deeper down.
- The same check applies inside a worktree: the gate checks the checkout it runs in.

**Not in scope:** running `npm install`, or changing the lock file.

**Done when:** after a pull that changes the lock file, the next session start leaves the main checkout passing `npm run check` without a manual step, and a stale tree reaches the gate as that one clear message, both covered by unit tests on the pure core and the thin shell with a fake process runner.

Batch state machine incl. Conditioning, Stuck and rewind

Lifecycle from architecture §4.3: ordered → brewing → conditioning / stuck → on_tap / cancelled.

- Exhaustive handling of every `StepOutcome` kind and blocker kind (compile-time `never` check)
- Commands: retry, skip, answer, recipe, rewind, cancel
- Rewind records the commit SHA per repository and appends `batch.rewound`

**Done when:** every transition has a test, and adding an outcome kind without handling it fails the type check.

Schemas: recipes, brewer frontmatter, foedrum.jsonc, models.jsonc

Split from #4, which now covers events, step outcomes, out-doc frontmatter and the multi-repository model (#47).

Zod schemas, through the internal wrapper in `src/schemas/` (ADR 0004, ADR 0005), for:

- Recipe files (brewers-and-recipes), including the serving-volume recipes (#44) and the test-first structure (ADR 0017)
- Brewer frontmatter (brewers-and-recipes)
- `foedrum.jsonc` and `models.jsonc`, read through `src/formats/` (ADR 0020)
- House yeast files under `.foedrum/house-yeast/` (ADR 0018), if they have frontmatter

Same approach as #47: test-first with stubs that throw `not implemented` (#25), exhaustive discriminated unions, generated JSON Schema files added to the reproducibility check.

**Done when:** every schema has valid and invalid fixture tests, the JSON Schema files are generated reproducibly, and `foedrum.jsonc` and `models.jsonc` get editor autocompletion through their `$schema`.

Supervisor: leases, deadlines, stall detection, reminders

One generic liveness mechanism instead of special-case stuck handling.

- Leases renewed by running attempts; expiry → attempt lost → retry policy
- A deadline per attempt; stall detection (no progress for N turns or M minutes)
- Conditioning reminders
- Invariant I5: a batch past its deadline becomes stuck within one tick

**Done when:** tests with a controllable clock cover expiry, deadline, stall and reminder paths.

State machine follow-ups from the review of #77

Follow-up from the review of #77 (batch state machine, #9). The design-conformance lens raised these on its last pass. As agreed, they are tracked here rather than fixed in another review round.

## 1. A human `recipe` on an ordered or Conditioning batch does not record who issued it (major)

`batch.recipe_chosen` for a human now carries `by: 'human'` and `via`, but not the issuer's name. From Stuck, the accompanying `batch.resumed { by, via }` records the issuer. From ordered or Conditioning, no other event does. ADR 0019 says "Every command is recorded as an event with **who** issued it and **from where**."

Suggested: give the human variant the issuer, for example `{ by: 'human', issuedBy: NonEmpty, via: Surface }`. Then update decide, the fold, `schemas/event.json`, architecture §4.1, and the issuer test in `test/unit/decide.test.ts`, which expects `['batch.recipe_chosen', 'human', 'dashboard']`.

## 2. ADR 0025 does not say it amends ADR 0019 (minor)

ADR 0025 defers the per-command zod schemas that ADR 0019 promises, and it changes the shapes of `batch.recipe_chosen`, `batch.rewound` and `batch.cancelled`. Add "Amends 0019" to its header and its README row, and "Amended by 0025" to ADR 0019.

## 3. `step.scheduled` also ends a Stuck reminder; two texts say only Conditioning (minor)

Architecture §4.1 (the `deadlines` bullet) and the comment in `src/engine/sqlite-event-store.ts` on the `step.scheduled` case should both say "ends a Conditioning or Stuck reminder".

## 4. Test names say "the book" (minor)

`test/unit/decide.test.ts`: "refuses a recipe the book does not have" (twice) and "refuses a recipe the book no longer has". The glossary term is "the Brewery".

Platform layer: process trees, paths, executables, file locks

Isolate OS differences per architecture §13 and ADR 0010.

- Kill process trees: POSIX process groups; Windows `taskkill /T /F /PID`
- Resolve executables through PATH and PATHEXT
- Strict argument validation for commands that must be spawned through a shell on Windows
- Retry file and worktree removal on `EBUSY` / `EPERM`; clean up stale `index.lock` files
- Path comparison that respects case-insensitive file systems

**Done when:** tests pass on all three CI platforms, including killing a real tree of child processes.



**Read-only folders on Windows.** On Windows, folders can carry the read-only attribute (observed on 2026-10-14 for worktree folders and their `.git/worktrees/<name>` records). Deleting a read-only folder then fails with "Permission denied", so git cannot remove the worktree and batches would leave debris behind. The platform module's removal helper clears the read-only attribute recursively before deleting, retries briefly (like the file-lock retries), and has a test that creates a read-only folder and removes it.

Git commands aimed at the scratch tree can detach the enclosing worktree's HEAD

During #77 the issue session's worktree ended up on a detached HEAD while it ran mutants and red-proof checks in its scratch tree (`.foedrum/tmp/9/scratch/tree`). Commits made after that were not on the branch, so the first push stopped short; the session noticed, moved the branch and pushed again. Nothing was lost this time, but it could have been.

**Likely cause (not confirmed from the transcript):** the scratch tree lives inside the checkout. When `<scratch>/tree` exists but is not (or no longer) a repository, for example after an interrupted clone or a partial removal that left the folder (Windows read-only attributes), `cd <scratch>/tree && git checkout --detach <sha>` does not fail: git walks up to the enclosing worktree and detaches *its* HEAD. `git -C <scratch>/tree …` behaves the same way.

**Proposal**
- Every git command the brew-review skill runs in the scratch tree sets `GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES=<scratch>` (or uses `--git-dir`/`--work-tree` explicitly), so it fails instead of reaching the enclosing checkout. Spell this out in `.claude/skills/brew-review/SKILL.md` stage 0, step 5, including for ad-hoc scripts a session writes for the mutation check.
- The gate blocks `git push` from a checkout whose HEAD is detached, with one line saying so. (A session pushes a branch, never a detached HEAD.) Pure check on `git symbolic-ref`'s output with a fake runner (ADR 0021).

**Done when:** a git command aimed at a scratch tree that is not a repository fails instead of touching the worktree, and a push from a detached HEAD is blocked with a clear message; both have tests.

Property tests for invariants I1–I6

doctor: a container tool that does not answer its version is not available (CI red on Windows)

CI on main is red since #97: `check (windows-latest, node lts/*)` fails `test/integration/doctor.test.ts:15` twice in a row (run 38805629722, attempts 1 and 2), while the same leg passed on the PR. The runner image has a `docker.exe` (`C:\Windows\system32\docker.exe`) that does not answer `--version`; the probe is killed after `VERSION_TIMEOUT_MS` (10 s, the test took ~10.9 s) and doctor prints:

```
Container: docker of unknown version at C:\Windows\system32\docker.exe; the container level is available
```

Two defects:

1. **Doctor logic** (`src/cli/doctor.ts`, the container choice around line 190): a container tool that is on PATH but does not answer its version counts as "the container level is available". Treat it like git and claude: there but not answering means not usable. Report it as such (for example `Container: docker at <path> does not answer its version; the container level is not available`) and fall through to the next candidate (podman before docker stays). 2. **Integration test** (`test/integration/doctor.test.ts:42`): it assumes every container tool it finds answers with a version. The container is optional and what a machine has differs (ADR 0021), so the test must accept the "does not answer" line as well as a versioned one.

Ordered batches need a routing deadline so I1 holds without an exemption

Found by the property tests of #14 (PR #95): **an Ordered batch has no deadline until it is routed**, so the I1 property has to exempt it. I1 (architecture §4.4) says every non-terminal batch has exactly one pending action with a deadline. As it stands, an order whose routing never happens (the router crashed, a label was never read, the engine restarted between `batch.ordered` and `route`) sits in Ordered forever without a word, and I5 cannot catch it because it has no deadline to miss.

**Proposal:** `batch.ordered` sets a routing deadline, like `step.scheduled` sets a step's. The store's `deadlines` index holds it, and routing (`batch.recipe_chosen`) or entering Conditioning replaces it. When it passes, the supervisor gets the batch Stuck with a `routing` reason (retry routing, choose a recipe, cancel), which also gives the human a reminder. Then the I1 property drops its exemption for Ordered.

Decide it in an ADR that amends 0025 (lifecycle) and 0027 (supervisor), merging origin/main before choosing its number. Test-first: the I1 property without the exemption is the red step.

**Done when:** the I1 property has no exemption for Ordered, and a unit test shows an unrouted batch becoming Stuck within one tick after its routing deadline.

Test budget: measure CPU time, so load from other sessions doesn't block pushes

The push gate fails a push when a unit test file runs over its 5 s budget (#87, #93). With three sessions in parallel, and especially during a session's mutation run, the machine sits at 100 % CPU. Unrelated unit files then go over budget on wall-clock time alone, and the push is blocked until the load drops. On 2026-10-16 this blocked both pushes of #102: first three unit files, then four, none of them chaos files. Each time the session had to wait and retry by hand, which goes against running sessions unattended.

The budget is meant to catch slow tests, not a busy machine.

**Proposal:** measure each file's budget in **CPU time** of its test process, or in CPU time plus a small allowance for I/O, instead of wall-clock time. A file that is genuinely slow still fails, whatever the load. Alternatives for the session to weigh:
- Re-run only the over-budget files once, after the run, and fail only if they're over again. Simple, but it still depends on the load.
- Scale the budget by the load average. Not available on Windows, so no.

Keep the 15 s ceiling for `test/property/` and `test/chaos/` on the same measure. `npm run check` overall stays under 20 s on a quiet machine.

**Test-first:** a unit test with a fake clock or CPU source. A file that waits (low CPU, long wall time) passes; a file that spins over budget fails.

**Done when:** the budget no longer blocks a push because of load from other sessions, and a genuinely slow file still fails the check and the gate.

Process runner: cap the output it collects

The process runner in `src/platform/processes.ts` (#12, PR #84) collects a child's output with no size limit: every chunk is appended to `stdout` or `stderr` and to `output`, so it is held twice. Before #84, the worktree cleanup ran git through `execFile`, which stopped at `maxBuffer` (1 MiB by default).

A command run against untrusted repository content can write far more than that before its deadline. Examples: a large `git diff` or `git log -p`, a hook or credential helper that writes without end, or a brewer's `claude` stream. Memory then grows until node runs out of heap, and the engine or the SessionStart cleanup crashes. The deadline does not bound this.

Found by the security lens in the review of #84 and moved here, because the runner's current callers (git with a 60 s deadline, the check's steps, `npm ci`) produce bounded output.

**Done when:**
- The runner takes a `maxOutputBytes` option with a sensible default (a few MiB).
- When the limit is passed, the runner kills the tree as it does at the deadline and reports it apart from an exit code. One way is `killed: 'too-much-output'`, extending `Killed` and `whyKilled`. The other is to keep only the last N bytes, as `deps-sync` does for its message. Pick one and record why.
- The behaviour is unit-tested with the fake spawner, and has an integration test with a real process that writes without end.

The real brewer runner (#11) must not land before this.

Test layers: refuse process starts in npm test's processes (ADR 0021)

Since the per-file budget counts CPU time (#108, PR #110), it no longer catches a unit test that starts a process. The child's CPU time is its own, and the test process uses almost none waiting for it. `scripts/check-test-layers.ts` catches only direct imports of `node:child_process` or the process runner. A test that starts a process through a module it imports is left to review. The ADR of #110 names this as a follow-up.

**Proposal:** the preload that `npm test` already loads in every test process (`scripts/test-cpu-time.ts`) also refuses to start processes in the layers `npm test` runs (`test/unit/`, `test/property/`, `test/chaos/`, ADR 0021). In a test process (`NODE_TEST_CONTEXT` set), it replaces `spawn`, `spawnSync`, `exec`, `execSync`, `execFile`, `execFileSync` and `fork` of `node:child_process` with functions that throw a clear error. The error names ADR 0021 and `test/integration/`. `npm test` then fails at the call, with a stack trace that shows which import started it.

Notes:
- **ES module namespaces are read-only.** The patch has to work for `import { spawn } from 'node:child_process'` as well as for the default export. Check whether patching the CommonJS module object before anything else loads covers named imports, or use `module.register` hooks. Verify it; don't assume.
- **The preload is also loaded in the runner process,** which must keep starting the test processes. It already returns early outside `NODE_TEST_CONTEXT`.
- **`test:integration` doesn't load the preload,** so integration tests are unaffected.

**Test-first:** a unit test with injected fakes for the patching. An integration test runs a unit-layer fixture that starts a process through an imported module and asserts that `npm test`-style options fail it with the ADR 0021 message.

**Done when:** a unit, property or chaos test that starts a process, directly or through any import, fails `npm test` with that message, and `check-test-layers.ts`'s comment and the ADR of #110 point to it.

Run the local gate without npm: under 150 ms per non-git call

Follow-up to #24 / #30.

## Why
Since #30 the local gate hook runs before every Bash and PowerShell call, with no `if` filter (a filter missed a push after a heredoc). It runs as `npm run --silent hook:gate`, which costs about **0.5 s per non-git call** on Windows (Node 24.20.0, npm 11.19.0, median of 30 runs):

| Command | Median |
|---|---|
| `node -e ""` (baseline) | 61 ms |
| `node scripts/precheck.ts` | 106 ms |
| `npm run --silent hook:gate` | 507 ms |

About 400 ms of that is the npm wrapper, which is only there to give precheck `npm_execpath` so it can start `npm run check` without a shell.

## What
- Run the gate as `node "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/scripts/precheck.ts"` without npm, for both the Bash and PowerShell hooks.
- precheck finds `npm-cli.js` next to `process.execPath` when it needs to run the check:
  - Windows: `<node dir>/node_modules/npm/bin/npm-cli.js`
  - macOS/Linux: `<prefix>/lib/node_modules/npm/bin/npm-cli.js`, where `<prefix>` is the parent of node's `bin` directory
- If it can't find `npm-cli.js`, precheck blocks with a clear message that names the paths it tried. It never lets the command through.
- The lookup lives in the platform module, or is injected so tests can use a fake file system (CLAUDE.md: OS-specific behaviour in the platform module only).
- Update `.claude/settings.json`, the wiring tests, `package.json` (`hook:gate` can go if nothing else uses it) and the "Local gate" section of CLAUDE.md.

## Done when
- [ ] Less than **150 ms per non-git call** (median of 30 runs, measured the same way as in #30) on Windows, and the numbers are in the PR.
- [ ] A missing `npm-cli.js` blocks with a clear message, covered by a test.
- [ ] Tested on Windows, macOS and Linux: a push with a failing test is blocked, and a non-git call passes.
- [ ] Test-first: red commit before the implementation.

Lease schema: require the canonical attempt key

Follow-up from the review of #82 (supervisor, ADR 0027).

**Make the lease schema require the canonical attempt key.**

#82 made a lease's `attemptKey` the canonical JSON text `["batchId","stepId",attempt]` (`src/engine/attempt-key.ts`, parts in `AttemptKeyParts` in `src/schemas/store.ts`). Claim a target-repository issue across Breweries before brewing it

**Model (from Edwin, 2026-10-16):** a target repository X is shared by a team. Every team member has their **own private Brewery** with its own engine, and each Brewery picks issues from repo X to brew. So several Breweries compete for the same issues. Once one Brewery picks an issue, the issue must be marked, so that no other Brewery and no person starts on it. Orders can also be created in a Brewery itself (not in any target repository) and broken into sub-orders that touch several repositories (ADR 0013). Those are private to the Brewery and need no claim on GitHub. Their pull requests land in the target repositories as usual.

**This changes the design:**
- `docs/architecture.md` today says issues in target repositories are "a triage source, never a work queue", and that Foedrum "never fixes, assigns, labels or closes anything in the target repository". In this model they are a work queue. That needs a new ADR, amending ADR 0008 (intake polls the Brewery) and the architecture section.
- **A claim on the state branch is not enough.** Each Brewery has its own state branch, so a claim there can't stop the others. The claim has to live in repo X on GitHub, and it has to be atomic between Breweries.

**Proposal (decide in the ADR):**
1. **An atomic claim in the target repository.** Create a git ref through the GitHub API, for example `refs/foedrum/claims/issues/<number>`. Creating a ref that already exists fails (422), so exactly one Brewery wins, with no race. The ref points at a small commit or tag that says which Brewery claimed the issue and when, without host or user names beyond the GitHub identity that made the ref. It needs push access to repo X, which team members have.
   - *Alternatives to weigh:* assignee or label only (not atomic: two Breweries can both add them); first claim comment wins by creation order (works with comment access only, but is only eventually consistent, so both Breweries may start before one backs off).
2. **A visible mark for people, set right after the claim succeeds,** through the effect ledger (ADR 0033), so that it's set exactly once across a crash:
   - assign the issue to the claiming Brewery's GitHub user, which is the GitHub-native "someone is on this";
   - the `foedrum: brewing` label;
   - a status comment naming the Brewery.
3. **What a Brewery picks.** The intake picks only issues that have no claim ref, have no assignee or are assigned to this Brewery's user, and match its filter (label, milestone or query, configured per Brewery and repository). An issue assigned to a person is that person's, which gives a simple team flow: assign it to yourself, and your Brewery picks it up.
4. **Release and takeover.** The claim ends when the batch ends: the pull request is merged or closed, or the batch is cancelled. Then the ref is deleted, and the label and assignee are updated. A claim whose Brewery went silent (no status update for a configured time) is **not** taken over automatically. A human releases it with a command, or by deleting the ref and unassigning, because two Breweries brewing one issue is the failure this issue prevents.
5. **Inside one Brewery** (ADR 0011, one active engine) the order is still pushed to the Brewery's own state branch before its first attempt, so a second engine of the same Brewery stops before any work.

**Brewery-native orders and sub-orders** need no claim, but their pull requests and branches in repo X must not collide with another Brewery's. Branch names carry the Brewery (ADR 0029's `foedrum/<batchId>/…` plus a Brewery prefix), so that two Breweries never push the same branch.

**Test-first:**
- a fake GitHub where two Breweries claim the same issue, and exactly one creates the ref while the other skips the issue;
- the mark set exactly once across a kill (a chaos case for #107);
- the intake skipping issues assigned to someone else or already claimed;
- release on merge, close and cancel.

**Related:** #103 (intake), #37 (drivers), #107 (chaos), ADRs 0008, 0011, 0013, 0024, 0029 and 0033.

Polling intake: order labelled issues and route Ordered batches (ADR 0008, 0032)

The polling intake is on the M1 roadmap ("Polling intake") and decided in ADR 0008, but had no issue. ADR 0032 (#98, PR #101) now gives it concrete work, so it gets one.

**Scope**
- Poll the Brewery behind the `Tracker` interface (architecture §3.1), with conditional requests (ETags), through the small in-house `fetch` client, authenticated by a fine-grained personal access token (ADR 0008).
- Turn a new labelled issue into an order: issue `decide`'s `order` command, which sets the batch's routing deadline (ADR 0032). The intake never appends `batch.ordered` itself.
- Route Ordered batches with `route` (`source: label` when a label names the recipe, `router` otherwise), including the batches a `retry` of a batch Stuck on routing sends back to Ordered with a new `routeBy`.
- An intake that is down or slow must not leave a batch silent: that is what the routing deadline is for. A chaos case (#15): kill the intake between `order` and `route`; the batch is Stuck on routing within one supervisor tick after its deadline.

Everything read from the Brewery is untrusted input.

**Open, to decide in the session:** the polling interval and backoff on rate limits; how a changed or relabelled issue maps onto an existing batch; whether the routing interval becomes configurable per Brewery here or with the reminder interval.

**Done when:** a labelled issue in a fake tracker becomes an Ordered batch with a routing deadline and is routed; a batch sent back to Ordered by a retry is routed again; unit tests with a fake `Tracker`, and an integration test against a recorded GitHub response.

Intake, part 2: the GitHub TargetTracker and IssueMarks, with ETags and rate-limit backoff

## How it works

The intake claims target-repository issues and marks them (ADR 0043, ADR 0050), but reads and writes GitHub only through two engine interfaces with no GitHub implementation yet: `TargetTracker` (open issues, pull request states) and `IssueMarks` (assignee, label, comments). This issue implements both on the GitHub client, with conditional requests (ETags) so an unchanged poll costs no rate limit, and decides how often to poll and how to back off on a rate limit.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  I["intake pass"] --> T["githubTargetTracker"]
  D["driver effects"] --> M["githubIssueMarks"]
  T --> R["conditional reads: ETag cache, Link pages"]
  M --> R
  M --> C["GitHub client"]
  R --> C
  C -->|"403 or 429 rate limit"| P["paused until reset: requests fail fast"]
```

The rest of #103 that was here (Brewery issues and routing, the intake in `foedrum serve`'s tick, the chaos case, `foedrum order`, relabelled issues and the routing interval) moved to #145. The open questions and review inputs are in #103's comments.

- [ ] **GitHub `TargetTracker`:** the open issues of a target repository, in pages, with ETags; how a pull request stands (open, merged, closed), with ETags.
- [ ] **GitHub `IssueMarks`:** assignees, assign, labels, add and remove a label, find the Brewery's own comment by its marker, comment.
- [ ] Each one stops when its signal aborts, with a test per implementation (from the #137 review).
- [ ] **Open questions settled in an ADR, each with a recommendation:** the polling interval, and the backoff on rate limits.

Attempt settings: deny a push with git options before the subcommand

## How it works

This is about the settings file the brewer runner writes for each attempt (ADR 0046). Its deny rules are the last word on what a brewer's tools may do. Every attempt denies `AskUserQuestion`, and `git push` in each shell the brewer may use (`alwaysDenied`, `src/schemas/attempt-settings.ts`): `Bash(git push *)` and `PowerShell(git push *)`.

Those rules match only a command that *starts* with `git push`. With a broad allow rule such as `Bash(git *)`, a model steered by untrusted text (an issue body, a file of the target repository) can still push with git's own options in front: `git -C . push`, `git -c x=y push`, `git --git-dir=… push`. Pushing is always the engine's job (brewers-and-recipes §1).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["allow: Bash(git *)"] --> C{"deny: Bash(git push *)"}
  C -->|"git push origin"| D[denied]
  C -->|"git -C . push origin"| P[runs: a push]
```

Found in the review of #165 (security lens). Until it is done, ADR 0059 refuses brewers with the `noPush` guard, so no brewer claims a guard the engine does not hold.

The first live run of `foedrum serve` with a real claude brewer (Windows, 2026-10-18) went Stuck on a finished, correct change: `attempts exhausted at brew after 1: the out doc brew.md is invalid: ✖ Unrecognized keys: "questions", "blockerKind"`.

GitHub only through gh's own login: Foedrum never holds a token

## How it works

Foedrum never holds a GitHub token. It reaches GitHub only through the maintainer's own `gh` login (`gh auth login`, which stores the credential in the OS keyring), for the API and for git pushes. Today `serve` reads `GH_TOKEN` or `GITHUB_TOKEN` (ADR 0063) and `src/github/client.ts` sends it as a bearer header (ADR 0008). A token in an environment variable is readable by every process started from that shell and ends up in sessions, logs and scripts. One credential system, owned by `gh`, removes that.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C["GitHubClient: rest and graphql, ETags, rate-limit pause"] --> T["transport: gh api --include"]
  T --> K["gh's login in the OS keyring"]
  G["git push: state branch, bottle branches"] --> H["credential helper: gh auth git-credential"]
  H --> K
```

- [ ] **The client's transport is `gh api`.** `GitHubClient` keeps its interface (`rest`, `graphql`, `GitHubAnswer`, `GitHubRateLimited`). Its one request path runs `gh api --include --method <m> -H <header>... <path> --input -` with an argument array and no shell, the body on stdin. Status, headers and body are parsed from stdout. `gh` exits 1 on any status of 300 or more, but still prints the status line and headers, so a 304 (ETag) or a 404 is an answer, not a failure. The timeout, the response size limit and the rate-limit pause stay where they are (ADR 0052). `api.github.com` stays the default host; `githubApi` maps to `gh`'s `--hostname` for GitHub Enterprise.
- [ ] **No token anywhere in Foedrum.** `GitHubClientOptions.token`, serve's `GH_TOKEN` and `GITHUB_TOKEN` and their refusal line go. Foedrum never runs `gh auth token`. `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `GH_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN` and `GITHUB_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN` stay out of the brewers' environment, as now.
- [ ] **doctor checks `gh`.** `gh` is a required tool: installed, a supported version, and `gh auth status` logged in to the host. It also checks that git's credential helper for that host is `gh` (`gh auth setup-git`). If it isn't, doctor names the helper git uses instead and recommends the fix. serve refuses without a login, with the line to run.
- Moved to #204: **brewers never reach `gh`** (the permission ceiling and a brewer's allowlist refuse `Bash(gh *)`, and doctor's isolation line says what the permissions-only level leaves open). ADR 0073 records the decision; #204 implements it.
- [ ] **ADR 0073** records the decision. It supersedes ADR 0008's fine-grained PAT, and ADR 0063's token variables, and says why the research choice of no `gh` runtime transport is reversed: one process per call is nothing at a poll every 30–60 s, and no token is ever handled. A GitHub App (later milestone) is a second login kind behind the same transport.
- [ ] Tests: unit tests of the transport's parsing (200, 304, 404, a rate-limited 403 with its headers, a body over the limit) with captured `gh` output, through the process runner the client takes. One integration test against the real `gh`, which tests our parsing, not GitHub: it runs against a local fake GitHub (gh's `github.localhost` through `HTTP_PROXY`, with a synthetic login in a configuration folder of its own), never against github.com.

Done when `foedrum serve` runs on a machine where `gh auth login` and `gh auth setup-git` were done once, with no token in any environment variable, file or log, and `doctor` reports both.

A recipe whose brewer produces commits but that does not end with `{ "action": "openPullRequest" }` goes on tap with "No pull request" (ADR 0059 allows on tap without a pull request). That branch was the only ref to the brewer's commit, so the work is left as a dangling commit that `git gc` will drop. Nothing warned anyone.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  B["brew: cellarman commits"] --> T["on tap, no pull request"]
  T --> C["cleanup: removes the worktree, deletes foedrum/3-1/brew/4"]
  C --> D["the commit is dangling"]
```

- [ ] **The cleanup never deletes the only ref to a batch's task tree.** If a batch ends with commits on its task tree that no push recorded (a recipe loaded before this rule, or a cancel), the cleanup keeps that branch and says so, as it keeps a worktree with changes.
- [ ] Red first: a unit test for the refusal with plain recipe data, and one for the cleanup's decision in its pure core.

Which of the two is enough is the session's call. My recommendation is both: the refusal states the rule, and the cleanup rule guards the work whatever the recipe does. One mechanism: a batch's commits always end up in a pull request or on a branch that's kept.

## How it works

Found in the consultant review of #231. On the sandboxed isolation level (macOS Seatbelt, bubblewrap on Linux and WSL2), Claude Code approves **every** Bash command that runs inside the sandbox, whatever the allow rules say. Claude Code's sandbox documentation (code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing, "Sandbox modes"):

> Claude Code approves a command automatically, with no prompt, when the command runs inside the sandbox.
> Auto-allow mode works independently of your permission mode setting, with three exceptions: plan mode, […] and server-side classifier review of sandboxed commands in auto mode.
> `autoAllowBashIfSandboxed` still defaults to `true`.

`dontAsk` is not one of the exceptions. Deny rules and content-scoped ask rules still apply. The attempt settings (`src/brewers/attempt-settings.ts`, ADR 0042/0046) write `sandbox: { enabled, failIfUnavailable, allowUnsandboxedCommands: false }` and never set `autoAllowBashIfSandboxed`. So on that level a brewer's `tools.allow` doesn't limit its shell at all, only its deny rules do. That undoes ADR 0062 (git without a fixed subcommand), ADR 0082 (`gh`, `git credential`), and the "Your shell runs only" line of #222 for every sandboxed brewer. The docs also say sandboxed commands may read "most of the machine, including credential files", so `gh auth token` or `cat ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml` would run there.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C["brewer's Bash command"] --> S{"inside the sandbox?"}
  S -->|"yes, autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true (default)"| R["runs, allow rules not consulted"]
  S -->|"no"| P["dontAsk + allow rules"]
  R -.->|"fix: autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: false"| P
```

- [ ] The attempt settings write `"autoAllowBashIfSandboxed": false` whenever they enable the sandbox, so the allow rules decide under `dontAsk` on every level. The schema (`src/schemas/attempt-settings.ts`) requires it.
- [ ] Red first: a unit test on `attemptSettings` with `sandbox: true`.

A run-out usage window makes the batch Stuck on environment, not a retried failure

## How it works

When a Claude subscription's usage window runs out, claude refuses every request until the reset. Claude Code's error reference (code.claude.com/docs/en/errors, "Usage limits") gives the messages:

> `You've hit your session limit · resets 3:45pm`
> `You've hit your weekly limit · resets Mon 12:00am`
> `You've hit your Opus limit · resets 3:45pm` / `You've hit your Sonnet limit · resets 3:45pm`
> "Claude Code blocks further requests until the reset time shown in the message."

With `stream-json` the message is in the `result` field. The runner's rule (ADR 0047) reads an error the result reported as a retryable failure, so a run-out window uses up the step's retries and the batch goes Stuck on a failure that says nothing about the cause. The refused requests cost no tokens, and `foedrum retry` after the reset recovers, but the lane and the status comment mislead.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  R["result: You've hit your session limit · resets 3:45pm"] --> T{"today"}
  T -->|"retryable failure"| F["retries used up, Stuck on a failure"]
  R --> N{"after this issue"}
  N -->|"blocked + environment"| S["Stuck: usage limit, resets 3:45pm"]
```

- [ ] The runner recognises the limit messages from the docs' texts, never from a test against claude (CLAUDE.md). The exact `result` shape (subtype, any status field) is settled from the docs and recorded in the ADR.
- [ ] Such an end is `blocked` + `environment`, naming the limit and the reset text as claude gave it; no retry. `foedrum stuck` and the status comment show it.
- [ ] Red first: a stream fixture built from the documented message, through `settleAttempt`.
- [ ] An ADR amending 0047.

Scope brewers' file-tool rules to the worktree in the attempt settings ## How it works **Touches the brewer runner's attempt settings** (`src/brewers/attempt-settings.ts`, `src/schemas/attempt-settings.ts`): the `--settings` file the runner writes for each attempt, the only settings a brewer's `claude` loads (ADR 0046). A brewer's bare `Read`, `Edit` or `Write` rule allows that tool anywhere on disk, and a bare `Grep` or `Glob` rule lets it search anywhere. The read guard hook of #40 cannot cover brewers, because the runner's `--safe-mode` turns off the hooks of the `--settings` file as well. Claude Code's own rules can: under `dontAsk`, `Read(./**)` allows only the worktree. This issue makes `attemptSettings` write scoped rules (ADR 0048, "Brewers"). ```mermaid flowchart LR B["brewer tools.allow
Read, Edit, Write, Grep, Glob"] --> S["attemptSettings"] S --> F["settings file
Read(./**), Edit(./**), Write(./**)"] F --> C["claude, dontAsk, --safe-mode"] C -->|"path inside the worktree"| OK["allowed"] C -->|"outside, .., a junction"| NO["denied"] ``` ## What - `attemptSettings` turns bare `Read`, `Edit` and `Write` into `Read(./**)`, `Edit(./**)` and `Write(./**)`, and a bare `Grep` or `Glob` into `Read(./**)`. `--tools` still decides which tools exist. - The `AttemptSettings` refinement refuses a bare file-tool rule (`Read`, `Edit`, `Write`, `MultiEdit`, `NotebookEdit`, `Grep`, `Glob`). - An integration test against the installed `claude` with the fake Messages API, like those in `test/integration/read-guard.test.ts`, for `Edit` and `Write`. A write outside the worktree, with `..` and through a junction, is denied, and a write inside is allowed. That file already verifies `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob`. - `docs/brewers-and-recipes.md` and architecture §10 and §13 then say this is in place: they currently mark it "not yet in `attemptSettings`". ## Done when - [ ] A brewer whose allowlist has a bare `Read`, `Edit`, `Write`, `Grep` or `Glob` gets a settings file whose rules allow those tools only inside the worktree. - [ ] A settings file with a bare file-tool rule cannot be written. - [ ] Test-first: red commit before the implementation. Follow-up to #40 (ADR 0048). ## Correction from Claude Code's docs (consultant, 2026-10-20) From code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions, re-read today: - "Claude Code checks file permissions against `Edit(path)` and `Read(path)` rules only. If you write a path rule for `Write`, `NotebookEdit`, `Glob`, or the legacy `MultiEdit` tool instead, Claude Code accepts the rule but never consults it, and warns at startup." - "`Edit` rules apply to all built-in tools that edit files." Read rules apply to Grep and Glob on a best-effort basis. - "Claude Code doesn't warn about a tool-name rule with no path, such as a deny rule for `Write`; it matches that rule at the tool level everywhere." - `path` or `./path` is relative to the current directory: the worktree, for a brewer. - Symlinks and junctions: an allow rule applies only when both the requested path and the file it resolves to match. So **a bare `Write` (or `MultiEdit`, `NotebookEdit`) becomes `Edit(./**)`, never `Write(./**)`**, and a bare `Grep` or `Glob` becomes `Read(./**)`. The refinement also refuses a path rule for `Write`, `NotebookEdit`, `MultiEdit` or `Glob`, since Claude Code would never consult it. ADR 0049 and architecture §10 say `Write(./**)`, so the ADR of this issue amends 0049. The demo brewer's own `Write(./**)` is one of those never-consulted rules.

driveNow drops the other ended runs of a pass when recording one end throws

Found by the correctness lens in the review of https://github.com/EdwinBekaert/foedrum/pull/275, and pre-existing: it is not introduced by that pull request.

`driveNow` in `src/engine/driver.ts` takes every ended run off its queue at once with `ended.splice(0)`, then records them one by one through `issue({ kind: 'finish', ... })`. If recording one of them throws (deciding or appending the finish fails, for example because the event store refuses an event or the disk is full), the throw leaves `driveNow`. The ends after it in that pass are already gone from the queue. Their `runs` entries are also gone, or are removed when the loop reaches them. So those attempts are never recorded and their leases are never released. They come back only when the supervisor finds the lease expired, loses the attempt and retries it.

Scenario: two runs end in the same pass. Recording the first throws. The second run's successful end is lost, and its attempt is retried after a lease's wait.

Suggestion: take ended runs off the queue one at a time (shift inside the loop), or catch per end and report it as a notice, so that one failing record does not drop the others.

- [ ] Recording one ended run that throws drops none of the others in the same pass; a unit test with two ends, the first of which fails to record, shows the second recorded and its lease released.

## How it works

The state worktree is where the Cellar writes the Brewery's state branch: at every step boundary the flush builds a commit there (`write-tree`, `commit-tree`) and pushes it (`src/engine/state-branch-git.ts`, ADR 0024). git creates `index.lock` in that worktree's git folder while it writes the index, and a git that is killed leaves it behind. The attempt worktrees remove a stale lock in their repair (ADR 0029, `removeStaleIndexLock`, `src/platform/index-lock.ts`); the state worktree has no such repair. So a Cellar killed during a flush can never start again: its start's signing check runs `write-tree` and stops on the lock.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  F["flush: write-tree in the state worktree"] -->|"SIGKILL, power loss, closed terminal"| L["worktrees/state/index.lock left"]
  L --> S["next start: checkSigning's write-tree"]
  S --> X["Unable to create …/index.lock: File exists, serve stops"]
```

**Seen on CI:** run 39579197252 (#295's first run, windows-latest, node 24), `test/integration/demo.test.ts`. The demo kills the Cellar mid-attempt; the restart printed `foedrum serve: git write-tree failed: fatal: Unable to create '…/demo/brewery/.git/worktrees/state/index.lock': File exists.`, and the batch never went on tap (`the code host has 0 pull requests, not 1`). A rerun passed: it depends on where the kill lands. The demo integration test also timed out locally in several sessions on 2026-10-21; whether that is the same cause is worth checking.

This also settles the second half of #174 (moved here): two drivers on one Brewery (the Cellar and an interactive session, ADR 0019) flushing one state worktree. A lock left behind and a lock another live writer holds look the same, so the repair needs to know whether any other writer can be in the worktree.

- [ ] Decide in an ADR: who may write the state worktree at a time (one flusher, a lock of Foedrum's own around the flush, or the driver lock), and so when an `index.lock` there is stale: under that exclusivity at once, without the 60 s age the attempt worktrees use.
- [ ] The state branch's start (before `checkSigning`) and a flush that meets the lock remove a stale `index.lock` through `removeStaleIndexLock`'s removal (`removeTree`), and say so in one line.
- [ ] Red first: a unit test with a fake git that answers `Unable to create … index.lock: File exists` and a lock file in a test folder, showing the start removes it and goes on; and that a lock held by a live writer is left alone.

A git commit killed in a state-branch flush leaves refs/heads/foedrum/state.lock, and every later flush fails

## How it works

The state worktree is where a driver writes the Brewery's state branch: every flush runs `git commit` there and pushes (`src/engine/state-branch-git.ts`, ADR 0024). ADR 0107 (#300, #305) made a start and a flush hold the state worktree's writer lock, so an `index.lock` left by a killed git there is stale at once and is removed. Only `index.lock` is removed, though.

**The gap:** a `git commit` killed after it took the lock on the branch ref, but before it renamed that lock into place, leaves `refs/heads/foedrum/state.lock` in the clone's common git folder (and possibly `HEAD.lock` in the worktree's git folder). The state branch's start meets a stale ref lock before it removes it: at worktree add, and the signing check's own ref

## How it works

ADR 0111 (#319) removes a stale `index.lock`, `HEAD.lock` and `refs/heads/foedrum/state.lock` at a start and a flush, under the writer lock. Two cases of the same kind are left:

1. **The start removes the locks after `openWorktree`.** When the state worktree does not exist yet (first start, or after it was deleted) and the clone has a stale `refs/heads/foedrum/state.lock`, `git worktree add -b foedrum/state …` fails with `cannot lock ref` before `removeLeftLocks` runs, and every start fails the same way. ADR 0111 names `worktree add` as one of the gits that moves the ref, so a kill during it leaves exactly this lock. `removeLeftLocks` asks both folders through the worktree (`rev-parse` in it), so it cannot run before the worktree exists; the common folder can be asked of the clone instead.
2. **The signing check's own ref.** `checkSigning` runs `git update-ref refs/foedrum/signing-check <sha>` and `update-ref -d` on every start, under the writer lock. A git killed there leaves `refs/foedrum/signing-check.lock` in the common folder, and every later start fails at that `update-ref`. Only Foedrum writes that ref, always under the writer lock, so ADR 0111's reason covers it; its "Nothing else" bullet leaves it out.

An attempt a route schedules doesn't get what sent it back: the failed reading or the findings

## How it works

A recipe sends a batch back to an earlier step in two ways (ADR 0064, ADR 0069):
- **A failed check:** `onFail: { goto, maxRounds }`. In Nip, a failed `green` reading sends the batch back to `implement`.
- **Findings:** `onBlocked: { findings: { goto, maxRounds } }`. In Nip, a Cellarman who finds one of the Gauger's tests wrong sends the batch back to `gauge`.

Either way, the attempt the route schedules records why (`step.scheduled` with `route: { from, why }`, ADR 0064). But **it doesn't get what sent it back.** A brewer's inputs come only from `order`, `step:<id>` (another step's out doc), `file:` or `lens:`, plus the human's answers after `needs_input` (`src/schemas/brewer.ts`, `src/brewers/prompt.ts`). A check step has no out doc, and the `goto` step's brewer doesn't declare an input from the step that blocked. So the Cellarman's second attempt starts with the same inputs as its first, without the failing checks, and may make the same mistake again. With `maxRounds: 1` the batch is then Stuck.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  I["implement attempt 1"] --> G["green check: test fails"]
  G -->|"onFail goto implement"| I2["implement attempt 2: same inputs, no reading"]
  I2 --> G2["green fails again"] --> S["Stuck"]
```

This matters more once brewers stop running the whole suite themselves: the Cellarman's definition of done then covers the tests of the code it changed, and the check step runs the rest (docs PR, 2026-10-22).

It goes between the per-prompt nonce tags as untrusted data (ADR 0041), never as an instruction, and has a size limit of its own.

Gravity readings: run check steps at the attempt's isolation level

## How it works

**Gravity readings** are a recipe's check steps. They run the target repository's commands (`npm test`, `make`, `./gradlew`) in an attempt worktree of their own, through the check runner (`src/checks/check-runner.ts`, ADR 0069). Brewers run inside Claude Code's OS sandbox at the `sandboxed` isolation level (ADR 0010). Check commands don't: they run as the Cellar's user, with network and home-folder access. And what they run is code an earlier brewer may have written: `npm test` runs the worktree's `package.json` script, which a brewer steered by an injected issue could have changed. With #194 the maintainer's GitHub login is in `gh`'s keyring, so such a script can act as the maintainer on GitHub.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  I["issue text, untrusted"] --> B["brewer step: OS sandbox"]
  B -->|"commits package.json, test files"| C["check step: no sandbox today"]
  C --> H["home folder, network, gh login"]
  C -.->|"this issue"| S["check in an OS sandbox with no network"]
```

**Decided on 2026-10-22:** a check step runs with **no network at all**. Foedrum drives the operating system's sandbox itself, with no new dependency:
- **Linux and WSL2:** `bwrap` (bubblewrap, which `foedrum doctor` already looks for at the sandboxed level) with no network namespace (`--unshare-net`), the home folder hidden, the worktree and a temp folder writable, the rest of the system read-only.
- **macOS:** `sandbox-exec` with a profile Foedrum writes per check: network denied, writes outside the worktree and a temp folder denied, reads of the home folder denied except the worktree.
- **Native Windows** (`unrestricted`, ADR 0010): brewers aren't OS-sandboxed there either, so a check adds no new reach; the check runs as today, and doctor says so.

Dependencies a check needs are installed before it, not by it: that's the repository's `setup` command, which nothing runs yet (#349). Anthropic's `@anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime` (what Claude Code's sandbox is built on) was weighed: it would add an allowlist proxy, which checks don't need with no network, and four runtime dependencies of a package marked beta.

- [ ] Red first, with a fake process runner: on Linux and macOS a check's command is started through the sandbox wrapper with the arguments above; on native Windows it is not, and the reading says so; a Brewery that requires the sandboxed level (ADR 0010) refuses check steps that would run below it, as it refuses writing brewers.
- [ ] An integration test on the platforms that have the sandbox: a check cannot write outside its worktree, cannot read a file planted in a test home folder, and cannot open a network connection. We test our wrapper's arguments against the real `bwrap` and `sandbox-exec`, not whether they work.

## What happened

The first order Foedrum brewed on itself (#374, Brewery batch `1-1` for #401) went Stuck at its red proof, through no fault of the Gauger. The Gauger added tests to `test/unit/attempt-settings.test.ts`, among them the line

```ts
const noAttribution = { commit: '', pr: '', sessionUrl: false };
```

and the red proof refused with:

> the red proof of step gauge failed: test "grants git status, add and commit in Bash to a brewer with git.commit" (and 1 more) passes before the implementation: a stub must throw, not return a value

That test is an old one the Gauger never touched. The second Gauger attempt stopped as `blocked (environment)`, rightly unable to see why.

## Why

`namesOf` (`src/checks/red-proof.ts`) gives `declares` the forms of a test's name to look for in the added lines: the name, the name without runner parameters, and **its last part after `::`, ` > `, `.`, `#`, `/` or `\`** (for `AddTest.adds`). For a sentence name that contains a dot, such as `… with git.commit`, the last part is `commit`. `declares` then finds `commit` standing as a whole word before `:` in the added line above, and the red proof judges the old, passing test as one the step added.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  N["test name: ... with git.commit"] -->|"namesOf: last part after the dot"| C["commit"]
  A["added line: { commit: '', ... }"] --> D{"declares: commit as a whole word, then ':'"}
  C --> D
  D -->|"yes"| P["old passing test counted as new: red proof refused"]
```

- [ ] Green: the last-part form is used only when the name has no space (a qualified name such as `AddTest.adds` or `tests/test_add.py::test_adds`), or another rule that keeps the qualified-name cases of the existing tests passing; the session picks it and says why.
- [ ] The existing red-proof tests stay green.

brewer-written files] --> S{setup} S -- today --> P[execProcess
network + home + /run + Keychain] S -- this issue --> B[check sandbox, network kept
home and /run hidden, Keychain denied,
writes only in the worktree] ``` ## The proof (CLAUDE.md, Security) The review of #378 found the path that #349 said to wait for. In a later step's worktree, setup runs build files a brewer may have committed. A batch merges its base before green, so its pull request opens up to date

## How it works

A batch's steps commit to its **task tree**, a branch that starts at `origin/<base>` when the batch is ordered (ADR 0063). The `green` step runs the repository's checks on it, and `openPullRequest` pushes it and opens the pull request (ADR 0071). Nothing brings in what merged into the base while the batch was brewing, so the pull request can open behind the base, or conflicting with it.

**The proof.** #431, the second order Foedrum brewed on itself (#374), opened behind main with a conflict in `test/unit/serve-config.test.ts`: #416 and #418 had merged during the brew of about 15 minutes. The consultant merged main by hand.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  I["implement"] --> M["merge origin/base into the task tree"]
  M -->|"clean"| G["green checks the merged code"]
  M -->|"conflict"| S["Stuck: conflicts with base in files"]
  G --> P["openPullRequest"]
```

Decided on #412 (2026-10-23, decision 4): the merge comes before green, so green checks the code the pull request will hold.

- [ ] A clean merge, or nothing to merge, goes on to green; a conflict aborts the merge and leaves the batch Stuck with the files it conflicts in (`conflicts with <base> in <files>`), options as for any Stuck batch. Resolving it is the Blender's, later.
- [ ] Main moving between green and the push is left to CI; the pull request is opened on what green checked.
- [ ] Red first, with real git in a scratch repository: a base that moved cleanly, one that conflicts, and one that did not move.

A repository's `setup` (`npm ci`, `dotnet restore`) runs only in a **check step's** worktree, before its checks ([ADR 0140](https://github.com/EdwinBekaert/foedrum/blob/main/docs/adr/0140-a-repository-s-setup-runs-before-a-check-step-s-checks-with-the-network.md), [ADR 0158](https://github.com/EdwinBekaert/foedrum/blob/main/docs/adr/0158-a-repository-s-setup-runs-in-the-check-sandbox-with-the-network-kept.md)). So a brewer's worktree has no `node_modules`, and even with `tools` allowing `npm run lint` the command could not run. Brewers write code blind: the Gauger and Cellarman of every trial so far reported "my shell only runs git status, git add and git commit", and the Cellarman's prompt says it need not run lint or format at all. **The proof.** Batch `7-1` (#292, the second order Foedrum brewed on itself, #374): green #1 failed on the typecheck (a type error in a test the batch wrote), implement #2 fixed it but left one line the formatter would have split, and green #2 failed on lint. Batch `1-1` (#401) passed only because its change was three lines. ```mermaid flowchart LR I["implement: writes code blind
no node_modules, no lint"] --> G["green: typecheck, lint, test"] G -->|"fails"| I2["implement #2: fixes blind"] I2 --> G2["green #2 fails on format"] --> S["Stuck"] I -.->|"this issue"| R["brewer runs format, lint, typecheck, tests itself"] ``` - [ ] A repository's `setup` also runs in a brewer's attempt worktree before the brewer starts, in the same sandbox as a check step's setup (ADR 0158; native Windows unsandboxed and recorded, as for checks), so the worktree has the repository's dependencies. Say what it costs per attempt (time, disk) and whether a later step's worktree can reuse an earlier one's install. - [ ] A failed or unstarted setup ends the attempt `blocked` on the environment with the setup's reading, before any model tokens are spent. - [ ] The default Cellarman and Gauger say to run the repository's format, lint, typecheck and the tests they touch when the repository's tools allow it, instead of "you don't need to run lint or format"; the green step stays the gate. - [ ] `docs/design/recipes/configuration.md` shows the `tools` a repository adds for that (for Foedrum: `npm run lint`, `npm run typecheck`, `npx biome format --write `, `node --test `), within the ceiling. - [ ] Red first: an attempt plan for a repository with a setup runs it in the brewer's worktree; a failing setup blocks the attempt with its reading. Run a recipe's parallel group: lens steps side by side

## How it works

A recipe's steps run one after another today. The schema already has a **`parallel`** step (`src/schemas/recipe.ts`: brewers that run side by side), but the load refuses it (`step "…" is a parallel step, which the engine does not brew yet`, ADR 0053). Tasting through several lenses (#26) and the plan review's six plan lenses (#391) should not take six times as long: their Tasters only read, so they can run at once.

Split from #26 on 2026-10-23. Needs #26's lens steps first.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  G["green"] --> P["parallel group"]
  P --> T1["Taster diff/correctness"]
  P --> T2["Taster diff/security"]
  P --> T3["Taster diff/test-design"]
  T1 & T2 & T3 --> V{"group verdict"}
  V -->|"every verdict approves"| N["next step"]
  V -->|"a blocking lens asks for changes"| C["back to Cellarman"]
```

- [ ] The engine runs each child of a `parallel` group as its own attempt, with its own lease and deadline, and none of them writes the task tree (a child whose brewer produces commits fails the load).
- [ ] The group ends when every child ended. ADR 0168 says each child's time counts toward the recipe's budget, summed; whether a budget is built at all is #445 (split off on 2026-10-24, discuss first).
- [ ] The group's verdict is `approve` only when every child that returns a verdict approves; a blocking child's `changes` sends the batch back as a lens step does (#26).
- [ ] A kill mid-group resumes only the children that had not ended (invariants of `docs/design/engine/invariants.md`).
- [ ] Red first, with chaos tests on the kill; an ADR (number from the consultant) amending ADR 0053.

**Done when:** the seeded tasting-room pull request of #26, with its lens steps in one `parallel` group, reports each defect from its own concurrent attempt, and a kill during the group resumes the unfinished children only.

**See it:** in the tasting-room test (`test/unit/tasting.test.ts`), the five lens attempts all start before any ends. The demo Brewery recipe with a `parallel` group of three lens steps is #448 (split off on 2026-10-24).
